a_check_on_this_change_itself: Mapping the file does not make opening a connection more expensive, which was worth checking because a connection per operation means a map and an unmap per operation, and __munmap does appear in the profile. Median open-plus-first-statement on the real database: 0.150 ms with no map, 0.163 ms at 256 MiB, 0.100 ms at 2 GiB. The full map is faster, because the first statement's pages come from the map instead of from reads.

arms.name: mmap 256 MiB
arms.note: covers 45 percent of this machine's 564 MB store

arms.name: mmap 2 GiB
arms.note: SQLite maps at most the file length; 563 MiB mapped in practice

endpoints: read syscalls the daemon performs per directory open, from /proc/<pid>/io syscr
daemon resident set size, because mapped file pages are counted in RSS even though the kernel can reclaim them, and a bounded-memory release blocker is still open
known_trade_off: With a memory map, an I/O error on the database reaches the process as SIGBUS rather than as an error return. For a filesystem daemon that turns a bad sector into a disappearing mount instead of an error. This is the reason the change needs a decision record, not just a commit.

measured.fixture: the owner's own account on the development machine: 184,092 items, a 564 MB metadata database, an actual kernel FUSE mount. Not synthetic.

read_syscalls_per_second_during_the_post.note: the same workload in all three: the daemon's own activity in the first half hour after a start, with the file indexer idle at 0 percent CPU.
read_syscalls_per_second_during_the_post.spread: the 256 MiB arm: 23 samples, 385,532 to 401,434. The 2 GiB arm: 8 samples, 412 to 13,572, which is wide because the burst's own work varies.

reads_per_directory_open.method: median of nine opens of the same directory, background rate measured and subtracted; every repeat cost the same before the change, so this is a fixed cost and not a cold cache
reads_per_directory_open.why_not_zero: SQLite reads the write-ahead log with ordinary reads, not through the map. metadata.db-wal was 16 MB.

prediction.i_may_be_wrong_about: whether the 82 reads are SQLite at all. The evidence is indirect: no file descriptor position advances, which means positional reads, and SQLite is the only positional reader in the daemon. A counter in the daemon would settle it directly.
prediction.reads_per_open: today about 82; cache_size barely better, because a pilot on a copy of the real 564 MB database moved only 5.6 to 4.7 reads per lookup; mmap_size close to zero, because the same pilot moved 2,239 reads to 1.
prediction.resident_memory: RSS rises by up to the mapped working set, so I expect a visible increase, bounded by 256 MiB per connection and shared between them because the mapping is of one file. I predict PSS rises far less than RSS. If RSS rises by more than 256 MiB the explanation is wrong and the change does not ship.

question: Opening one directory on the mount costs about 82 database read syscalls, measured on the owner's machine and reproducible on every repeat. Does setting PRAGMA mmap_size on the store's connections remove those syscalls, and what does it cost in resident memory?
result: passed. Reads per directory open 82 to 11. The post-start read storm 875,000 to about 2,000 per second, a factor of roughly 400. Resident memory rose 63 MB, all of it reclaimable file pages.

second_prediction.occasion: The 256 MiB arm halved the rate rather than removing it, which is the covered fraction of the file and nothing more.
second_prediction.prediction: A map covering the whole 564 MB file brings the rate below 40,000 reads per second, under a tenth of the 875,000 measured during the incident. If it does not, size is not the explanation and the change is wrong.

what_this_did_not_fix: The daemon still spends about a core for 16 to 25 minutes after every start. Profiling it (pkexec sysctl kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0, then eu-stack sampling only threads whose stack leaf is not futex/read/epoll_wait/syscall) found the cause: a new SQLite connection per operation. Of 16 computing stacks, 5 were in Store::open, 4 in closing a connection, 4 in sqlite3Prepare/yy_reduce, and only 4 in Store::with_children. An open plus one statement costs 0.10 ms against 0.002 ms warm. The fix is the pooled read connection ADR 0006 called a prerequisite; it is not in this change.
where_the_prediction_was_wrong: I predicted PSS would rise far less than RSS, because the map is of one file and is shared between the store's connections. It did not: RSS rose 63 MB and PSS rose 64 MB. Sharing between threads of one process does not divide PSS -- proportional set size divides a mapping between the processes that hold it, and only this process maps the database. The bound I set the prediction against was the right one and it held: the whole rise is file-backed and reclaimable, and anonymous memory actually fell by 16 MB.
why_it_matters: On 2026-09-16 the owner updated the OS and rebooted. GNOME's localsearch-3 re-crawled $HOME, which contains the mount, and cirroved burned about 93 percent of one core for 25 minutes at roughly 875,000 read syscalls per second. No file content was fetched (content_gets was 0), so the cost was entirely metadata lookups amplified by a crawler. A machine whose fan spins up for half an hour after every update loses its user.
